title: The Lantern Under the Pier

topics.value_lesson: Patient watching: some answers only appear if you sit quietly in the dark and wait

spine: Pip and the night-watch keeper follow a mysterious blue flash under the pier to discover how jellyfish make their own light in the dark.

lantern_word.role: What Pip calls the jellyfish's light (used in the final line)

segments.text:
Pip hurried down the wooden pier at dusk, hugging a borrowed notebook, and the boards went creak, creak, creak under their shoes.

"Careful!" called {keeper_name}, the night-watch keeper, from the little hut at the end. "That last board has opinions."

Pip stepped over it. "I'm here to sketch the light," Pip said. "If it comes back."

"Oh, it comes back," said {keeper_name}. "The question is whether it lets you look."

The sea below was black as a cupboard with the door shut. Pip leaned over the rail, pencil ready.

Then it happened.

A small blue pulse bloomed in the dark water. A lantern switching on. Pip gasped and pressed the pencil to the page.

Gone.

"Did you see it?" Pip whispered.

"I always see it," said {keeper_name}. "I've just never seen what makes it."

Pip stared into the black. Nothing. Not a ripple.

Then the whole sea exploded.

SPLOOSH!

Something enormous burst up beside the pier, and the splash went up like a fountain and came down like rain. Pip got it full in the face.

"Sorry! Sorry!" said a whiskery voice. A young harbour seal hauled his chin onto the lowest board, beaming. "Barnacle," he said, by way of hello. His nose bumped the pier. The pier wobbled. Pip's pencil nearly went overboard.

And all around Barnacle, the water glittered. Thousands of tiny lights, scattered by the splash, drifted and swirled like sparks off a bonfire.

"Plankton," breathed Pip, sketching fast. "The plankton glows."

Barnacle looked down at the shining water around his whiskers. Then he looked back up at Pip, and his eyes went round.

"Pip," he said slowly. "The water is looking at you."

"The deep end," said Pip. "Where the big water hides."

They crept to the pier's end, where the boards stopped and the sea dropped away into black. Barnacle flopped along beside them, trying to tiptoe. A seal cannot tiptoe. Every step went thump.

Pip leaned over the edge, notebook ready.

"There!" Pip whispered.

Below them, a jellyfish pulsed through the dark. Its bell squeezed and stretched, squeezed and stretched, pushing it along like an umbrella opening and closing. And it was see-through. Clear as a window. Clear as bathwater.

Pip squinted. Inside the jellyfish, right in the middle of its see-through tummy, a tiny green spark glowed.

"It's glowing!" Pip said. "But it's green, not blue. And it's inside."

"Maybe it ate a light bulb," said Barnacle.

"It ate plankton," said {keeper_name}, coming up behind them. "A glowing one. The jellyfish swallowed it whole, and it's still shining in there. Like a lantern swallowed by a window."

Pip sketched fast. The jellyfish drifted past, green spark blinking inside its clear belly, and its bell kept pulsing. One squeeze pushed it forward. One squeeze scooped up dinner. One squeeze breathed. Three jobs, one squeeze.

But it did not flash blue.

"That's not our light," Pip said slowly. "Something else made that blue flash. Something bigger."

The jellyfish pulsed away into the dark, carrying its little green lantern with it.

"Under the pier," said Pip. "Where the shadows keep secrets."

They ducked down the wooden steps and crouched between the pylons. The water here was still and dark, and the air smelled like salt and old rope. Barnacle squeezed in beside them, which meant there was suddenly much less room.

"Sorry," he whispered. His whiskers tickled Pip's ear.

Then Pip saw them.

Jellyfish. Dozens. Hundreds. A whole jelly bloom, drifting past like slow snowfall. Moon jellies, pale and round, each one pulsing its bell in no hurry at all. They came in a silent parade, too many to count, tumbling gently over each other like bubbles in a bath.

"It's snowing jellyfish," Pip breathed.

Pip reached out one finger, slow as anything, toward the nearest one. The jellyfish felt the water move and pulsed away, quick and soft, like a soap bubble escaping.

No flash. No blue light. Nothing.

"Why won't they glow?" Pip whispered.

SPLOOSH.

Barnacle had fallen in.

He surfaced a moment later, snorting water out of his nose, looking extremely pleased with himself. "I'm fine!" he announced.

And then Pip saw it. Everywhere Barnacle had splashed, the jellyfish near him pulsed and flashed. A tiny blue blink. Then another. Then another.

"They glow when they're bumped!" Pip said, grabbing the notebook. "Not all the time. Only when something touches them!"

Barnacle looked at the jellies blinking around him. "I did that?"

"You did that," said Pip. "But you didn't make the big flash. Something else did."

The bloom drifted on, dark and silent, keeping its secret.

"What did you find?" Barnacle whispered, dripping on Pip's shoes.

Before Pip could answer, {keeper_name} clicked off the red torch. The dark came down like a lid. "Now we wait," she said. "Quiet as pebbles."

They sat. Pip hugged the notebook. Barnacle tried to sit quiet as a pebble, which for Barnacle meant wobbling like a jelly in a jar.

The black water gave nothing back. Not a ripple. Not a spark. Pip's eyes began to invent lights that were not there.

"I don't like waiting," Barnacle breathed, and his whiskers tickled Pip's ear. "Waiting is just standing still with your hopes up."

Then his stomach rumbled. Rumble. Rumble. Loud as a boat engine in the quiet.

"Sorry," he whispered. "All this thinking about plankton."

He slid off the pier, meaning to be silent, and made the smallest splash of his entire life. It was still an enormous splash.

Pip held their breath. The sea settled. Nothing.

Then, out in the black, Barnacle's nose bumped something soft and clear, something that had been drifting there all along, invisible as a held breath.

FWOOSH.

Blue fire bloomed under the water, silent and huge, a lantern switching on inside a cupboard the size of the sea. Barnacle yelped and spun, and every way he turned the dark lit up around him, ring after ring of cold blue flame.

"Pip!" he shouted. "The water found me back!"

And far below the light, something much larger turned, slow and curious, and looked up at them out of the deep.

The great shape turned once, slow as a moon, and slid away into the dark it had come from. The rings of blue flame folded in after it, smaller and smaller, until the last one winked out like a candle pinched between fingers.

"Come up," Pip called softly. "Before you set it off again."

Barnacle hauled himself onto the pier, streaming, and flumped down beside the notebook. "I didn't touch it," he said. "Much."

Pip opened the notebook flat on the boards. {keeper_name} clicked the red torch on, just a whisper of light, and held it over the page. Pip's pencil moved fast. A bell like a clear umbrella. Trailing arms. A bloom of blue in the middle.

"Label it properly," said {keeper_name}, leaning in. "A discovery nobody can read is only half a discovery."

So Pip wrote, tongue between teeth. Bioluminescence — light made by a living thing. Plankton — the tiny drifters that sparkled when Barnacle splashed. And along the bottom, in Pip's best writing: a jelly bloom, when the jellies gather like lanterns at a window.

"There," Pip said. "Pinned down. It can't be forgotten now."

{keeper_name} took the pencil and, in the corner, drew a small round seal with enormous splashes and very surprised eyes. Barnacle inspected it, whiskers twitching.

"That's me," he said, pleased. "I look brave."

"You look surprised," said Pip.

"Bravely surprised."

They walked home along the pier, boards going creak, creak, creak, the notebook tucked safe under Pip's arm. Out in the black water, one small blue pulse bloomed, far off, saying goodnight. Pip didn't need to sketch it. The page was warm in Pip's mind, a {lantern_word} small enough to fit in a pocket, and keep.

The great shape turned once, slow as a moon, and slid away into the dark it had come from. Barnacle watched it go with his chin on the boards.

"It has cousins," Pip said suddenly, closing the notebook. "{keeper_name}, doesn't it? Things that carry light the same way."

"So they say," said {keeper_name}, eyes crinkling. "Along the shore path, this time of year."

That was enough for Pip. "Come on."

They left the pier, boards going creak, creak, creak behind them, and took the shore path where the grass grew tall and salty. Barnacle galumphed along the waterline beside them, because paths, he explained, were for creatures with no flair.

Then Pip stopped.

Above the grass, a tiny green light blinked on. Off. On again. Then another. Then a dozen, drifting and winking over the dark field like slow sparks that had learned patience.

"Fireflies," Pip breathed.

One floated close, and Pip held still as a pebble while it pulsed, right beside Pip's ear. On. Off. A little lamp carried through the night, same as the jellyfish below — one in the black water, one in the black air, each making its own light out of nothing but being alive.

"You're doing it too," Pip whispered to it. "Bioluminescence."

The firefly blinked, unimpressed, and wandered off.

Down at the waterline, Barnacle reared up for a farewell. "Tell it I said—" he began, and overbalanced, and his goodbye splash went up like a fountain and came down like rain. The fireflies scattered, laughing in light, if light can laugh.

Pip laughed too, and wiped the drops off the notebook, and looked back once — at the sea, at the grass, at all those small lamps going on and off in the dark.

"Goodnight, {lantern_word}," Pip said, and carried the glow of it all the way home.

gathered_but_unused: Many deep-sea jellyfish make their own light through a chemical reaction called bioluminescence, using a light-producing molecule and an enzyme inside their own bodies
Sunlight only reaches down about 200 metres in the ocean, and below that the water is completely dark, yet glowing jellyfish live all the way down
Some jellyfish flash bright blue light when something bumps or touches them, which can startle a predator or attract an even bigger hunter to chase the attacker away
A jellyfish's body is mostly water and almost completely see-through, so you can sometimes see its last meal glowing inside its stomach if that meal was a glowing creature

The crystal jellyfish, Aequorea victoria, gave scientists two glowing tools, aequorin and green fluorescent protein, which are now used in laboratories to make living cells light up so scientists can watch them work
When conditions are right, huge numbers of jellyfish can appear together in one place, and this gathering is called a jelly bloom
A jellyfish moves by squeezing its bell, the dome-shaped top of its body, pushing water out behind it, and this pulsing is also how it breathes and eats, since it has no heart, brain, or bones
Tiny drifting creatures called plankton are the main food of many jellyfish, and jellyfish trail long stinging tentacles through the water like fishing lines to catch them
